column3: Arrange the five fundamental stages of a standard curling slide delivery in chronological sequence.
column4: The sequence starts stationary in the hack and ends after the stone is released with rotational handle.
column5: A proper slide delivery begins with setup in the hack, a clean forward press, the backswing and leg drive, sliding out on the slider foot, and the smooth release with handle rotation before the near hog line.

column3: Arrange the four-player curling team positions in their traditional throwing order from first to last.
column4: The front end throws before the back end; the team captain traditionally throws the final pair.
column5: In a standard four-person game, the Lead throws stones 1-2, the Second throws 3-4, the Third (Vice-Skip) throws 5-6, and the Skip throws 7-8. The Alternate serves as the fifth player in reserve.

column3: Arrange the concentric circles and boundaries of the curling house from the central pin outward.
column4: The button lies at the absolute dead center and is encircled by three progressively larger colored rings.
column5: The house consists of the central button (usually one or two feet in diameter), followed by the 4-foot circle, the 8-foot circle, and the outermost 12-foot circle. Any stone clearing beyond the back line is out of play.

column3: Arrange these curling delivery weights in order from lowest kinetic energy to highest velocity.
column4: A stone designed to rest in front of the house is thrown softer than one designed to smash out guards.
column5: Draw and guard weights are finesse shots with low speed. Takeout speeds increase through hack weight, control weight, and board weight up to maximum-velocity peel weight.

column3: Arrange the painted ice markings encountered by a sliding curler traveling from the delivery end to the target end.
column4: The stone is delivered out of the hack and must be released before the near hog line.
column5: A curler pushes from the delivery Hack, crosses the near Back Line, releases the stone before the near Hog Line, glides past the mid-sheet Centre Line, and targets the far Hog Line and house.

column3: Arrange the key steps an ice maker follows when preparing competition ice before game play.
column4: Scraping flattens the sheet before water droplets are sprayed onto the surface and trimmed.
column5: Proper ice prep requires blading and scraping to flatten the sheet profile, mopping debris, spraying a base water pebble, spraying a fine top pebble, and nipping the pebble tips with a razor blade.

column3: Arrange the historical evolution of the Free Guard Zone rule in competitive curling chronologically.
column4: The rule expanded from three protected stones to four then five before addressing center guards with the no-tick rule.
column5: The FGZ was introduced in 1993 with 3 stones, increased to 4 stones internationally, raised to 5 stones in 2018, and updated in 2022 to the No-Tick rule to preserve offensive play.

column3: Arrange these historic Olympic curling events in chronological order.
column4: Chamonix 1924 was the earliest Olympic curling competition; mixed doubles entered at PyeongChang 2018.
column5: Great Britain won the first men's Olympic gold at Chamonix 1924, Lake Placid 1932 was a demonstration, Nagano 1998 restored curling as a full medal sport, and PyeongChang 2018 added mixed doubles.

column3: Arrange the physical components of a competition curling stone from top to bottom.
column4: The colored plastic handle sits on top; the contact running ring glides along the pebble on bottom.
column5: At the top sits the handle and colored cap, secured by the central bolt passing through the granite body. Around the stone's widest perimeter is the striking band, and underneath lies the ground concave running edge.

column3: Arrange these legendary Canadian skips in chronological order of their first Brier national championship.
column4: Ernie Richardson dominated the 1950s and 60s; Brad Gushue captured his first Brier crown in 2017.
column5: Ernie Richardson won his first Brier in 1959, Al Hackner in 1980, Russ Howard in 1987, Randy Ferbey (as skip) in 2001, and Brad Gushue in 2017.

column3: Arrange the operational sequence of a single end in Mixed Doubles curling from start to finish.
column4: Pre-positioned stones are placed on the centre line before any rock is delivered by the players.
column5: Mixed doubles begins with positioning stationary stones (one guard and one house), followed by the first player throwing stone 1, the partner throwing stones 2, 3, and 4, the first player throwing stone 5, and then scoring.

column3: Arrange the skip's sweeping commands from least aggressive to maximum physical effort.
column4: Off tells sweepers to lift brushes completely; Hard demands maximum downward pressure for distance.
column5: Sweepers progress from Off (no contact) to Clean (hovering brush to clear frost), Sweep (steady brushing for line), Hard (full cardio for distance), and Carve (directional angle sweeping to influence curl).

column3: Arrange the sequence of measuring procedures used to settle a disputed point in the house.
column4: Teams start by visually assessing the house before calling the chief umpire and official gauge.
column5: Players first attempt a visual naked-eye inspection. If too close to call, an umpire is summoned to insert the measuring pin in the button, rotate the micrometer gauge arm, and declare an official ruling.

column3: Arrange the traditional sequence of post-game sportsmanship and curling club customs.
column4: The game concludes on the ice with handshakes before teams retire to the clubhouse lounge for broomstacking.
column5: Play ends when the trailing team concedes; players shake hands saying Good Game, confirm and sign the scorecard, return their stones to the corners, and join opponents for broomstacking drinks.

column3: Arrange the technological eras of curling brooms in chronological order from earliest to modern.
column4: Scottish brooms began as natural corn straw before horsehair and synthetic textiles took over.
column5: Early curling used stiff Canadian corn straw brooms, followed by hog and horsehair brushes, synthetic cordura nylon heads, the directional-fabric controversy of 2015 (Broomgate), and today's standardized WCF fabric.

column3: Arrange these legendary skips in chronological order of their first World Women's Curling Championship title.
column4: Elisabet Högström led Sweden to gold in the early 1980s; Silvana Tirinzoni dominated the 2020s.
column5: Elisabet Högström won World gold in 1981, Sandra Schmirler won her first in 1993, Anette Norberg in 2005, Eve Muirhead in 2013, and Silvana Tirinzoni in 2019.

column3: Arrange these famous Scottish curling historical milestones in chronological sequence.
column4: The Stirling Stone dates back to the early 1500s; the Royal Caledonian club established the sport's global rules.
column5: The Stirling stone bears the date 1511, Paisley Abbey records mention curling in 1541, Kilsyth Curling Club formed in 1716, the Grand Caledonian Curling Club was founded in 1838, and the first Scotch Cup world championship took place in 1959.

column3: Arrange the specific procedural requirements governing a wheelchair curling stone delivery.
column4: In wheelchair curling players release using an extender stick from a stationary chair without sweeping.
column5: The wheelchair must be brought to a complete stationary stop, feet lifted off the ice, the delivery cue stick engaged with the handle, the stone smoothly propelled by hand, and no sweeping is permitted anywhere on the sheet.

column3: Arrange these tactical curling shots from lowest tactical risk to highest risk of conceding multiple points.
column4: An open peel on an opponent guard carries very low risk; attempting an angle runback double is high risk.
column5: A clean peel of an unprotected stone is low risk. An open draw to the 8-foot is standard. A freeze against an enemy rock requires precise weight. A double takeout requires line and power. A thin angle runback double is high risk.

column3: Arrange these prestigious Grand Slam of Curling tournaments in the typical order they are contested during the elite curling season.
column4: The Tour Challenge typically opens the Grand Slam season in autumn leading toward the Players' Championship in spring.
column5: The Grand Slam season historically runs Tour Challenge (early fall), Masters, National, Canadian Open (mid-winter), and culminates with the prestigious Players' Championship in spring.

column3: Arrange these Canadian curling competitive tiers in progression from youth developmental play to senior national supremacy.
column4: U15 youth events precede U18 and U21 juniors before curlers qualify for the Brier or Scotties.
column5: Competitive curlers in Canada advance from U15 youth leagues to the Canadian U18 Championship, the Canadian U21 (Junior) Championships, U Sports collegiate competitions, and ultimately the men's Brier or women's Scotties.

column5: With a two-point lead and hammer in the final end, the skip's priority: 1) Peel opponent center guards immediately after FGZ, 2) Keep the four-foot clear, 3) Force play to the side wings, 4) Avoid clutter or freezes, 5) Make an open hit or throw through with the hammer for victory.

column3: Arrange the thermal levels of a dedicated curling facility from the coldest refrigerant zone to the warmest ambient air.
column4: The sub-floor brine pipes are the coldest; arena air above the spectator seating is warmest.
column5: Subfloor refrigeration pipes chill at -7°C (20°F), keeping the ice base around -5°C (23°F), the pebble running surface at -4°C (25°F), the air one foot above ice at 4°C (39°F), and ceiling air near 10°C (50°F).

column5: The hammer team announces the Power Play before stone delivery. The stationary stones are placed on the chosen wing: a corner guard in the free guard zone and a house stone biting the 8-foot and 4-foot on the tee line. The center line remains clear.
